Scientific nameAmmannia gracilis
Other namesRed Ammania, Pink Ammania, Delicate Ammania, Large Ammania
Minimum tank size20 gallons (~80 liters)
DifficultyMedium to difficult
LightingModerate to high
Optimal pH6.5 – 7.5
Optimal hardnessSoft-Medium
Optimal temperature72 – 79°F (22 – 26°C)
SubstrateNeeded
Can floatNo
Can be grown emersedYes
SizeUp to 20 inches (50+ cm)
Growth formStem
Growth rateFast
Placement in tankBackground
FertilizerNeeded
CO2Needed
PropagationVegetative and by seeds

Ammannia gracilis is endemic to Africa. It can be found in Guinea-Bissau, Gambia, Senegal, Guinea, Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger, and the Central African Republic.

It was first described in 1833 by Guillemin and Perrottet in “Florae Senegambiae Tentamen”. The genus name honours the German botanist and physician Paul Ammann (1634-1691); the species name “gracilis” is Latin for slender or graceful.
Ammannia gracilis is usually found in wetlands, marshes, floodplains, and areas with stagnant or slow-moving water, where it grows on sandy riverbanks and floodplains.

Ammannia gracilis requires a lot of space because of its growth potential. It is suited only to larger (especially tall) aquariums starting from 20 gallons (80 liters).

Even in such an aquarium, over time the plant will become so large that you will have no choice but to trim it.

In aquariums, this plant is commonly used as a classic stem plant, planted in dense groups along the sides and as a background plant due to its larger size. In aquascaping it can also serve as a focal point.

Under optimal conditions it grows fast. Once established, it may take only a few weeks before it is ready for propagation and/or trimming.

Do not allow the plant to reach the surface, or you may get a big tangled mass. Start trimming when there are 4-6 inches (10-15 cm) left to the water surface. You can safely shorten it by half; it will grow back quickly. Trim regularly to prevent overcrowding and promote bushier growth.

Planting

Avoid planting it in one large clump. Instead, plant stems about 2 inches (5 cm) apart and make sure no other plants shade it while it grows.

Plant it deep enough in the substrate to keep it from floating up; there is no special method or trick. Tip: use a pair of tweezers. Unlike some plants that can be left floating until roots develop, this is not advisable with Ammannia gracilis.

Propagation

  • By seeds. The flowers produce viable seeds, but this method requires a lot of time and effort and cannot guarantee results, so it is not popular among aquarists.
  • Vegetative (cuttings). This is the main method in aquariums. Simply cut off the stems and plant them, making sure each cutting is at least 2 – 3 inches (5 – 7 cm) long.

Dry start method

The Dry Start Method is an effective technique for growing this plant. Its main benefit is that it may supply large amounts of CO2 without extra equipment.

  • Instead of filling the tank with water right after planting, add just enough water to reach the surface of the lowest part of the substrate.
  • Using tweezers, carefully plant the stems into the substrate.
  • Cover the top of the tank with cling wrap to create a humid environment.
  • After approximately 5 to 8 weeks, flood the tank with water.

This method promotes initial growth before the transition to submerged conditions.

Ammannia gracilis is not a good choice for beginners due to its high light, CO2 and nutrient demands, and its need for stable water parameters. It is not a hardy plant, as some people claim; it is quite sensitive to temperature fluctuations and water quality.

  • Temperature: ideal 22 – 26°C (72 – 77°F). Sudden temperature fluctuations may result in leaf melting.
  • pH: prefers slightly acidic to neutral water, pH 6.5 to 7.5.
  • Hardness: prefers soft to moderately hard water; grows best at 2 – 10 GH.
  • Flow: does not like high flow. In nature it is not found in fast-flowing rivers or streams. Too much flow may make it melt within days.

Lighting

Ammannia gracilis is a very light-demanding plant. It needs a lot of bright light to reach its full growth potential, so use an effective lighting system giving at least medium-high light (30–50 PAR) with a standard photoperiod of 10-12 hours daily. The plant may melt if it does not get enough light.

Some opinions online suggest it can grow in low light, but even if the plant survives under such conditions, it will grow slowly and look feeble. The color will be mostly green with little to no red undertones, which is what aquarists are looking for.

Substrate

It prefers loose, nutrient-rich substrates. In nature it thrives in sandy soil along riverbanks and in flooded areas. A two-layered substrate, with a thin nutrient-rich base layer and fine gravel or sand on top, is a good choice.

CO2 and fertilization

CO2: supplementing CO2 is highly advisable. Without CO2, growing this plant can be quite challenging because it will show limp and elongated growth. It is crucial to keep CO2 and nutrients balanced for high-light plants; intense lighting without CO2 injection is not recommended, as it can lead to significant algae problems.

Fertilization: this is a fast-growing plant and requires adequate nutrients. A regular supply (2-3 times a week) of macro- and micronutrients is essential for growth and vibrant coloration. Nitrogen, phosphorus and iron are particularly important.

If you keep shrimp with this plant, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Description

A very long-stemmed, slender plant that can grow both emersed (above the water surface) and submersed (underwater). Its appearance changes drastically depending on the growth form.

  • Size: 10 – 20 inches (20 – 50 cm). The stem is thick and gives a robust appearance.
  • Growth form: in emersed form, the stem rarely grows completely upright; it tends to bend, curve and prostrate.
  • Leaves: sessile, entire-edged, arranged in a cross-opposite pattern. Emergent leaves are linear to inversely ovate, 2-6 cm long and 1-2 cm wide, olive-green. Submerged leaves are lanceolate, 7-12 cm long and 0.7-1.8 cm wide, with the upper surface olive-green to brownish-red and the lower surface intensely violet or red.
  • Flower: the inflorescence consists of 3-7 small flowers with 4 purple petals and either 4 or 8 stamens, growing in clusters.
  • Roots: thin, but the plant develops a relatively strong root system.

Problems

  • Melting: usually happens when the plant is moved from emersed to submersed conditions. If the plant you just bought has green, ovate leaves, it was grown emersed. Don't panic: in most cases it will regrow the leaves or continue growing with new submerged leaves.
  • Black leaves: often caused by a lack of light. Check your lighting and adjust it.
  • Excessive leaf shedding: caused by insufficient light, nutrient deficiencies, or both. Provide more light and fertilize regularly.

Benefits

  • Aquascape: an excellent decorative addition, commonly used in Dutch-style aquascaping, particularly as a focal point.
  • Hiding place: serves as cover and shade for invertebrates, small frogs and fish, including fry and shrimp.
  • Foraging place: acts as a buffet of biofilm, an ideal first food for newly hatched fry and shrimplets.
  • Prevents gas pockets: its well-developed root system helps break up anaerobic pockets in the substrate. Hydrogen sulfide pockets (H2S, smelling like rotten eggs) can be really dangerous to fish or shrimp.

Compatible tankmates

Fish: best kept with small, peaceful community fish such as neon tetras, killifish, swordtails, white cloud mountain minnows, zebra danios, cherry barbs, sunburst platies, Endler's livebearers, mollies, Otocinclus catfish and pygmy corydoras.

Shrimp: since the plant prefers slightly acidic water, choose species that prefer the same parameters, for example crystal red shrimp, blue bolt shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti.

Freshwater snails: ornamental snails should not be kept for a long time in low-pH water, as it harms their shells. If your pH is close to 7.0, almost any snail or dwarf shrimp can be kept, for example Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails.

Avoid or be careful: avoid fish that disturb the substrate near the plant or find it too palatable, e.g. silver dollars, Buenos Aires tetras, koi, goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey, clown loaches, African cichlids. Most crayfish and freshwater crabs are also a poor combination, as they may cut, eat and uproot almost everything in the tank.

Quarantine

Unless you are completely sure the plant is safe, for example it was grown in sterile laboratory conditions (in vitro) and the in vitro pot is undamaged and unopened, quarantine and disinfect it first to avoid contamination and poisoning. This plant is quite sensitive to bleach and hydrogen peroxide, so be cautious when using them.

Do not put a new plant into the tank right after buying it: it can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.), and may contain pesticide residues that are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Conclusion

The plant is stunning and decorative, but it demands special care, especially to preserve its reddish-brown coloration; in unsuitable conditions its hue may fade to ordinary green at best. Because of its size, keep it in an appropriately sized tank, as in small tanks it will reach the surface and shade neighbouring plants.
